c.tagline: Lermontov's Caucasus spa town of mineral springs and mountain air.

taxi.fareNote: Yandex Go is by far the cheapest and most reliable option; street-hailed taxis are unmetered, so agree a price before getting in. Note that most foreign bank cards no longer work in Russia—carry cash.

emergency.note: 112 is the unified emergency number; 102 police, 103 ambulance, 101 fire.

avoid.reason: No no-go districts in town itself, though onward travel toward some neighboring North Caucasus areas warrants checking current advisories.

hood_desc: The elegant spa core at the foot of Mount Mashuk, centred on the Tsvetnik flower garden, the Lermontov Gallery, the Aeolian Harp, Diana's Grotto, and the historic mineral-water pump rooms; the classic first-timer base for 'taking the waters'.

The city's lively main avenue, lined with shops, cafes, restaurants, theatres, and 19th-century architecture; the most central and convenient place to stay, walkable to both the resort park and the markets.

The wooded slopes and sanatorium belt below Mashuk, reached by cable car, with the eerie blue Proval underground lake, health spas, and panoramic views toward Mount Elbrus; a calm nature-and-wellness setting.

The original hot-springs settlement on the south side, a traditional, largely residential district with a big Cossack market and local mineral baths; an authentic, budget-friendly, less touristy feel.
A quiet residential area around Novopyatigorsk Lake with a sandy swimming beach and parks; relaxed and family-friendly, away from the resort bustle.

water.note: Quality varies; most visitors drink bottled water or the town's famed mineral-spring water.

transit.hours: Trams and marshrutkas run roughly 5:30 AM to 11:00 PM; service thins out late evening.
transit.note: Pyatigorsk has one of Russia's narrow-gauge tram networks plus city buses and marshrutka (shared minibus) routes; Yandex Go fills the late-night gap.
transit.pay: Pay the driver or conductor in cash on board (a flat fare per ride); contactless bank cards work on many trams and marshrutkas. There is no separate tourist card.

bus: Intercity coaches from Pyatigorsk Bus Station
train: Suburban elektrichka to Mineralnye Vody and Kislovodsk

tip.r: Rounding up or leaving about 10% at sit-down restaurants is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Caucasian Shashlik
food.desc: Lamb or pork threaded onto skewers, marinated with onion and grilled over vine or fruitwood coals. Served with raw onion, herbs and flatbread.

places.name: Shashlyki u Volodi
places.note: Widely named by locals as the best shashlik in town; indoor and garden seating, no frills.

places.name: Shashlychnaya No. 1
places.note: Caucasian grill house with a long-standing reputation for skewers cooked over real coals.

places.name: Kafe Pechorin
places.note: Reliable shashlik plus house lemonade, in a smarter setting close to the spa quarter.

food.name: Khychiny
food.desc: Karachay-Balkar flatbreads stuffed with cheese, potato or greens, griddled thin and brushed with melted butter. Cut into wedges and eaten with the hands.

places.name: Khychinok
places.note: Cafe specialising in khychiny, consistently well rated for the classic cheese-and-potato version.

places.name: Khinkalnaya-Shashlychnaya na Brodveye
places.note: Mountain-cuisine cafe on the main promenade doing khychiny alongside khinkali.

places.name: Verkhny Rynok food stalls
places.note: Market bakers sell khychiny hot off the griddle at the lowest prices in the city.

food.name: Khinkali
food.desc: Georgian pleated dumplings filled with spiced minced meat and broth. Grip the twisted top, bite a hole, drink the juice, then eat the rest.

places.name: Khinkalnaya-Shashlychnaya na Brodveye
places.note: Praised for khinkali done properly, with well-made dough and plenty of broth.

places.name: Shashlychnaya No. 1
places.note: Serves khinkali beside the grill menu; handy if the group wants both.

places.name: Kafe Pechorin
places.note: Georgian-influenced menu in a comfortable central room, good for a longer sit-down meal.

food.name: Khachapuri
food.desc: Cheese-filled Georgian bread, either the round Imeretian loaf or the boat-shaped Adjarian one topped with a raw egg yolk and butter to stir in.

places.name: Kafe Pechorin
places.note: Does both Imeretian and Adjarian versions; good stop after walking the Tsvetnik galleries.

places.name: Khinkalnaya-Shashlychnaya na Brodveye
places.note: Georgian breads baked to order alongside the dumplings and skewers.

places.name: Khychinok
places.note: Cheese breads of both Caucasian and Georgian traditions on one short menu.

food.name: Shurpa
food.desc: Clear, fatty lamb soup with big chunks of potato, carrot and herbs, simmered for hours. The standard first course at any Caucasian table here.

places.name: Shashlychnaya No. 1
places.note: Soups are made in quantity daily to go with the grill; shurpa is the one to order.

places.name: Shashlyki u Volodi
places.note: Home-style soups before the skewers, at the same unpretentious prices.

places.name: Verkhny Rynok canteens
places.note: Market canteens serve shurpa and lagman to traders from early morning.

food.name: Chudu
food.desc: Thin Dagestani stuffed pies filled with meat, pumpkin, curd or nettles, cooked dry on a hot pan and brushed with butter. Sold by the round.

places.name: Verkhny Rynok food stalls
places.note: Best place in Pyatigorsk for mountain pies made by Dagestani and Balkar bakers.

places.name: Khychinok
places.note: Serves several styles of stuffed North Caucasian flatbread in one place.

places.name: Khinkalnaya-Shashlychnaya na Brodveye
places.note: Rotating pies and breads alongside the main mountain-cuisine menu.

food.name: Pyatigorsk Mineral Water
food.desc: The city was built on its springs: warm sulphurous and cold narzan waters, each drawn at a set temperature and drunk from a spouted cup at the pump rooms.

places.name: Akademicheskaya Galereya
places.note: Historic colonnaded gallery above Tsvetnik, one of the classic places to take the waters.

places.name: Lermontovskaya Galereya and Tsvetnik pump rooms
places.note: Cluster of drinking galleries in the spa park, each tapping a different named spring.

places.name: Pitevaya Galereya (main drinking gallery)
places.note: Modern pump room serving several waters including Mashuk No. 19; free to drink.

food.name: Ayran
food.desc: Salted, whisked sour milk served ice cold, sometimes sparkling. The traditional Caucasian answer to a plate of grilled lamb on a hot day.

places.name: Verkhny Rynok dairy stalls
places.note: Farm ayran and fresh curd sold by mountain producers; the best version in the city.

places.name: Shashlyki u Volodi
places.note: Cold ayran poured by the jug to go with the skewers, as locals drink it.

places.name: Khychinok
places.note: Standard accompaniment to khychiny here, along with house compotes.

landmarks: Mount Mashuk
The city's 993-metre landmark peak, ascended by a Soviet-era cable car for sweeping views across the Caucasus foothills to snow-capped Elbrus.
Proval
A striking natural sinkhole with a turquoise sulphur lake inside Mount Mashuk, reached by tunnel and immortalised in Ilf and Petrov's satire.
Park Tsvetnik and the Lermontov Gallery
The elegant heart of the spa town, a flower-filled park anchored by a turquoise Art Nouveau iron-and-glass concert gallery from 1901.
Eagle Sculpture (Orjol)
A bronze eagle clutching a serpent on Goryachaya Hill, the beloved emblem of Pyatigorsk and the entire Caucasian Mineral Waters region.
Diana's Grotto
An artificial stone grotto of 1831 where Mikhail Lermontov danced at a ball just a week before his fatal duel.
Aeolian Harp
A graceful hilltop rotunda of 1831 that once held wind-played strings, now the classic viewpoint over the city and Elbrus.
Lermontov Museum-Reserve (Lermontov's Cottage)
The humble thatched cottage where the poet spent his final months in 1841, preserved with his belongings as Russia's oldest literary memorial.
Lermontov Duel Site
A solemn obelisk in the woods at the foot of Mashuk marking the spot where Russia's great Romantic poet fell in 1841.
Academic (Elizabethan) Gallery
A white stone colonnade of 1851 crowning the spring where fashionable society once took the waters, framing postcard views of the town.
Spassky Cathedral
The city's gleaming five-domed cathedral, destroyed under Stalin and painstakingly rebuilt by 2012 as the spiritual centrepiece of downtown Pyatigorsk.

train.note: No international trains. Pyatigorsk is on a branch off the main North Caucasus line, with through sleeper carriages to Moscow taking about 24 hours and frequent local trains to Kislovodsk, Yessentuki and Mineralnye Vody, where the region's airport is. Foreign cards often fail on the RZD site.

bus.note: No international coaches. Buses and marshrutka minibuses from the Pyatigorsk bus station link the spa towns of the Caucasus Mineral Waters group and run to Nalchik, Vladikavkaz and Elbrus for the mountains. Tickets are sold at the terminal. Check current travel advisories for the wider North Caucasus before planning.

ferry.note: Pyatigorsk is inland in the Caucasus foothills with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Kislovodsk
half.blurb: A spa town about 40 minutes away centers on a large landscaped park and mineral springs used for treatment since the 19th century.

half.name: Yessentuki
half.blurb: A mineral-water resort town roughly 25 minutes from Pyatigorsk bottles sulfate-alkaline spring water and draws visitors to its pump rooms and sanatoriums.

half.name: Zheleznovodsk
half.blurb: A small spa town set against forested slopes about 20 minutes away is known for hot mineral springs and the Ostrovsky Baths building.

full.name: Mount Elbrus
full.blurb: Europe's highest peak rises about four hours southwest, with a cable car climbing partway up its slopes toward glacier viewing platforms.

full.name: Dombay
full.blurb: A ski resort deep in the Caucasus Mountains roughly four hours away offers cable cars up to alpine ridgelines with views toward Georgia.
